tldr: We demonstrate that even an ultra-lightweight, quasi-steady fluid simulator that completely ignores wakes and added-mass history is sufficient to learn a general closed-loop controller for a soft robotic fish and transfer it directly to an outdoor pool, simply by bounding the frequency of the action space.
hero_caption: The complete pipeline of this study. Tail dynamics are identified in air and a quasi-steady fluid model is identified in water. The reinforcement learning policy drives the motor via a band-limited trajectory generator (TG). The exact same learned controller is deployed onto the real hardware in an outdoor pool, successfully achieving target reaching and tracking.
overview:
Robotic fish with flexible tails are quiet and well-suited for observing marine life. However, because they are underactuated systems—possessing more degrees of freedom than actuators—where the entire body bends continuously, controlling them freely has been notoriously difficult. Reinforcement learning (RL) can discover complex swimming behaviors, but it demands millions of trial-and-error steps. High-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulators are far too computationally expensive for RL. Meanwhile, fluid models built into fast physics engines like MuJoCo are merely "stateless and quasi-steady" low-fidelity models that ignore vortex formation, shedding, and past fluid history. Whether policies learned in them could ever transfer to hardware (Sim-to-Real) remained a long-standing question.

The authors tackled this with an unconventional perspective: instead of making the simulator more accurate, why not confine the controller's actions to the regime where the model is valid? Because stateless fluid models compute thrust solely from instantaneous velocity, direct RL quickly exploits a simulation loophole—generating thrust via small-amplitude, high-frequency micro-vibrations (flutter) that look nothing like natural flapping to human eyes. To counter this, the authors independently performed system identification on tail elasticity and fluid drag coefficients, and then inserted a frequency-bounded Trajectory Generator (TG) into the action space. This physically prevents the policy from deviating beyond the frequency band (1 to 4 Hz) identified in real-world experiments.

Thanks to this constraint, a single neural network policy trained on a crude fluid model transferred zero-shot—without any hardware parameter tuning—to a real robotic fish deployed in an outdoor pool. In hardware experiments, the robot demonstrated not only high-precision static target reaching, but also disturbance rejection (such as surviving pokes from a stick), acquisition of out-of-distribution targets (e.g., directly behind the fish), and dynamic tracking of manually moved targets. This work vividly proves that the Sim-to-Real gap can be bridged through constraints on the controller side rather than demanding excessive physics inside the simulator.
contributions: Demonstrated the first zero-shot Sim-to-Real transfer of a closed-loop RL controller for a soft, underactuated robotic fish using a stateless, quasi-steady fluid model that completely neglects wakes and fluid history.

Proposed a staged, two-step system identification pipeline based on tail oscillation in air and free-swimming data in water, cleanly separating passive structural stiffness from hydrodynamic drag to achieve faithful dynamics.
Introduced a band-limited Trajectory Generator (TG) into the action space, physically preventing the policy from exploiting the high-frequency flutter artifacts inherent in low-fidelity fluid models.

Demonstrated general, robust task performance in an outdoor pool environment, including target reaching, disturbance rejection, tracking of out-of-distribution goals (targets up to 175 degrees behind and far away), and dynamic moving-target tracking.

sections.heading: Introduction: Why soft robotic fish are hard to control, and how to fix it
sections.summary: Flexible robotic fish offer great compliance, but learning whole-body control is challenging due to the underactuated coupling of elasticity and fluid dynamics. CFD is too slow for RL and simple fluid models deviate from reality, but this study bridges the gap by strictly band-limiting the controller's action space.
sections.details:
Recent quadrupedal and humanoid robots have mastered agile, dynamic whole-body control through reinforcement learning. In robotic fish, however, control has largely remained restricted to straight-line swimming or switching among a few hand-crafted, fixed swimming strokes (gaits).

The bottleneck in learning whole-body control for fish robots stems from their underactuated nature with passive flexible joints. Even with only a single motor, interactions among the elastic body, driving tendons, and surrounding nonlinear hydrodynamics produce complex S-shaped bending waves. This dynamics is fundamentally different from rigid-body robots where each joint angle can be explicitly commanded. While RL holds the potential to master such intricate motion, it demands millions of steps of data, making learning exclusively on hardware impossible.

Turning to simulation, CFD can resolve realistic vortex-laden flows, but its computational cost per step is far too high to feed the massive sample appetites of RL. Conversely, fast simulators like MuJoCo rely on stateless, quasi-steady approximations that discard fluid memory and vortex shedding, making them physically remote from real fluid behavior. This paper demonstrates that even with such a low-fidelity simulator, one can acquire a versatile, real-world controller by placing an upper bound on the frequencies the policy can generate.

sections.heading: Related Work: The trade-off between simulation fidelity and control freedom
sections.summary: Underwater simulation spans a spectrum from heavy CFD solvers to fast, quasi-steady approximations. Prior work either relied on immense CFD computations or merely tuned fixed gaits; this study ventures into the unexplored territory of combining low-fidelity simulation with unconstrained whole-body gait generation.
sections.details:
Simulation environments for underwater robotics have always faced a strict trade-off between computational cost and fidelity (realism). At one extreme lie high-fidelity CFD solvers that resolve wake vortices. End-to-end RL inside CFD can achieve agile zero-shot transfer to hardware, but training a single policy demands hours of high-performance computing, and platforms have typically been limited to fully actuated multi-joint robots with sensors at every articulation.

At the other extreme are stateless, quasi-steady models that approximate hydrodynamic forces purely from instantaneous rigid-body velocities. Prior work with these low-cost simulators successfully deployed tendon-driven eel-like robots, but restricted the task to straight-line forward swimming. Furthermore, most studies achieving target tracking on real robotic fish granted the policy minimal authority—merely adding or subtracting a steering offset angle to a fixed, human-tuned swimming pattern.

While some studies have trained whole-body target reaching in digital twins, they remained confined to simulation and assumed privileged states, such as tail curvature that cannot be measured on physical soft hardware. This study sets itself apart by using a low-fidelity simulator while granting the policy full authority to synthesize the swimming gait, taking only real-world measurable sensor signals as inputs to achieve actual hardware deployment.

sections.heading: Experimental Platforms: The physical robotic fish and its MuJoCo digital twin
sections.summary: The physical platform is a soft robotic fish flexing an elastic PLA tail plate via antagonist tendons driven by a single motor. The simulator uses MuJoCo, modeling the fish as a rigid head and a 5-link elastic hinge chain paired with an ellipsoid-based quasi-steady fluid model.
sections.details:
### III-A Hardware Configuration
The physical platform is a tendon-driven soft robotic fish propelled by a head and a tail fin (Fig. F3).
- **Head**: A Raspberry Pi 5 onboard computer is housed inside a sealed, 3D-printed head filled with mineral oil to adjust buoyancy.
- **Drivetrain**: A Dynamixel XW430-T200-R servo motor is located in the flooded mid-body, rotating a pulley in position-control mode. Antagonistic tendons wound in opposite directions are routed along a 1.8 mm thick flexible PLA plate (the tail). A single motor controls both stroke amplitude and frequency, producing smooth traveling waves along the tail.
- **Sensors**: The robot uses only its internal motor encoder, an Adafruit BNO055 IMU in the head, and a 3D-printed AprilTag on top to measure position and orientation via an overhead camera.

### III-B Simulation Configuration
MuJoCo was chosen as the RL environment. Mass, center of mass, and moments of inertia were faithfully extracted from the CAD model. The fish is modeled as a rigid head connected to a 5-revolute-joint tail chain via torsional springs and dampers.

Hydrodynamics relies on MuJoCo's default ellipsoid-based quasi-steady fluid model. This extends a flat-plate tumbling model to 3D; drag forces depend solely on instantaneous rigid-body velocities, maintaining no wake history or ambient fluid states. As described next, this study expands the conventional 5-coefficient model into a total of 15 coefficients distributed across the robot's distinct body segments.

captions.F3: Hardware configuration of the robotic fish. (A) Transparent CAD rendering showing the Raspberry Pi 5 in the oil-filled head, the submerged Dynamixel motor in the center, and the antagonistic tendon routing running from the pulley along the flexible PLA tail. (B) The fully assembled physical fish deployed in an outdoor pool.

sections.heading: System Identification: Disentangling structural elasticity from hydrodynamic drag
sections.summary: Passive tail stiffness and fluid drag were identified in two isolated experiments. Tail stiffness and damping were first locked in via sinusoidal excitation in air, followed by optimizing 15 fluid coefficients across three body zones (head, tail, fin) using free-swimming water data.
sections.details:
### IV-A Tail Dynamics Identification
As a crucial first step, the tail's passive structural stiffness and damping were identified. Performing this identification in air first is vital: underestimating tail stiffness forces subsequent fluid identification to artificially inflate rotational fluid drag to compensate for the missing structural restoring torque.

Because static pull tests suffer from friction hysteresis, sinusoidal sweeps across four frequencies were applied at the motor shaft in air, isolating stiffness from the torque-angle frequency response. The identified shaft stiffness was approximately 0.98 N·m/rad (~3.8x higher than an idealized model's 0.26 N·m/rad), with viscous damping of ~0.011 N·m·s/rad. Using Euler-Bernoulli beam theory matching the tail's tapered height profile, this bulk stiffness was mapped across individual hinges from base to tip, spanning 2.99 down to 1.32 N·m/rad.

### IV-B Fluid Model Identification
Prior studies shared a single set of 5 fluid coefficients across the entire fish. However, increasing rotational drag to suppress head yawing inadvertently froze the flapping of the fin, which is needed to generate thrust. To solve this, the authors partitioned the body into three zones (head, tail, and caudal fin), assigning a total of 15 coefficients.

To decouple motor tracking errors, open-loop swimming trajectories recorded on hardware (replaying identical encoder profiles) were used. CMA-ES was applied to minimize trajectory tracking errors. In the identified parameters, the fin's rotational drag and Kutta lift coefficients were an order of magnitude larger than the head's. This occurs because the stateless model compensates for missing real-world vortex thrust through coefficient inflation. Furthermore, to eliminate an artifact where the simulated fish swam backward during initial strokes, acceleration-phase errors were penalized 4x more heavily to absorb added-mass effects.

### IV-C Motor Identification
Post-deployment, the actual Dynamixel motor parameters (delay, proportional position gain, and back-EMF velocity limits) were identified in the time domain from recorded encoder logs to see how far the training model had diverged. The results revealed that the actuator model assumed during RL training resembled an ideal, zero-delay, infinitely stiff servo—strikingly different from reality. That the controller never collapsed despite this mismatch is credited to the controller architecture detailed in the next section.

sections.heading: Control Architecture: Capping frequencies to prevent simulator exploitation
sections.summary: Because quasi-steady fluid models compute thrust from velocity squared, unconstrained control collapses into high-frequency micro-fluttering. By introducing a frequency-bounded Trajectory Generator (TG) into the action space, the policy is confined to the identified domain (1–4 Hz), naturally discovering realistic, large-amplitude strokes.
sections.details:
### V-A Control Challenge: The Simulation Loophole
MuJoCo's quasi-steady fluid model calculates hydrodynamic forces based on the square of instantaneous body velocities. Consequently, it cannot differentiate between moving with large amplitude at low frequency versus shivering with tiny amplitude at high frequency; both yield identical thrust. When RL directly commands motor angles (Direct Action), the policy inevitably exploits this loophole by converging toward high-frequency fluttering. This mode has nothing to do with real vortex-driven propulsion, causing catastrophic failure when transferred to hardware.

### V-B Trajectory Generator (TG)
The Trajectory Generator resolves this fundamental defect (Fig. F2). Rather than commanding raw motor angles, the policy outputs six parameters: base frequency $\omega$, offset $\theta_c$, and first- and second-order Fourier harmonic coefficients $(a_1, b_1, a_2, b_2)$. These parameters are smoothed via first-order low-pass filters with time constant $\tau = 0.1$ s, and the frequency $\omega$ is bounded below an upper limit of 4 Hz, matching the range identified in hardware experiments.

Because frequency is strictly capped, the only way for the policy to produce higher velocity (and thus thrust) is to increase stroke amplitude. As a result, the policy naturally learns large-amplitude, visible strokes that translate reliably to the physical fish.

### V-C Reinforcement Learning Setup
Policies were trained using Soft Actor-Critic (SAC). The observation space was strictly confined to 24 dimensions accessible by real sensors (encoder angle and angular velocity, IMU yaw rate, TG phase, past action history, and overhead camera relative target vector and latency). No privileged internal simulator states (such as precise tail curvature) were exposed to the policy.

Training progressed through a 10-stage curriculum across three phases: adding observation noise and communication latency, applying domain randomization (±5% to 20% on stiffness, damping, mass, and fluid drag), and widening the target angle range from a narrow frontal cone to ±60°, ±120°, and ±180°. The policy deployed on hardware was the one that completed the curriculum up to ±120°.

captions.F2: Overview of the reinforcement learning loop. Left: MuJoCo digital twin with 15 fluid coefficients across three body zones. Center: The Trajectory Generator (TG) smooths policy actions $u^*$ via first-order filters and outputs motor target angles $\theta_m$ while enforcing frequency bounds. Observations are restricted to real-world measurable states, driving the SAC algorithm on the right.

sections.heading: Hardware Experiments: Zero-shot transfer and disturbance robustness in an outdoor pool
sections.summary: In an outdoor pool (~5.5 x 2.7 m), the learned policy operated immediately without tuning. It achieved static target reaching, handled out-of-distribution backward targets, tracked moving figure-8 goals, and exhibited remarkable recovery against harsh disturbances like stick pokes.
sections.details:
### VI-A Experimental Setup
An overhead camera (~60 fps) mounted above an outdoor pool (~5.5 x 2.7 m) tracked AprilTags on the robot and targets, computing relative positions in the fish's frame and streaming them to the Raspberry Pi 5. The policy ran inference at 50 Hz, commanding the Dynamixel motor through updated TG parameters.

### VI-B Real-World Deployment Results
Trained purely in simulation, the policy steered the physical robot smoothly without any hardware tuning (Fig. F7 A). For targets 1.6 m away, the fish executed clean, large-amplitude strokes and closed in within 4.5 cm. Across 22 static target trials, it met the training success threshold (within 5 cm) in 11 trials, and stayed within 20 cm in 13 trials. The physical tail beat frequency settled at around 1.3 Hz, confirming steady low-frequency swimming free from high-frequency flutter.

### VI-C Out-of-Distribution Generalization and Disturbance Rejection
The hardware policy showed impressive resilience under conditions never seen during training:
- **Out-of-Distribution Targets**: When presented with targets far outside the training range (±120°, 2.5 m)—such as targets sitting nearly dead behind at +158° or -175°—the fish executed wide U-turns, closing to within 2.1 cm and 1.6 cm. It also reached distant goals placed 2.8 m away.
- **Dynamic Tracking**: When a target was manually moved by hand, the robot continuously tracked it, following a figure-8 trajectory smoothly for roughly 73 seconds (Fig. F7 B).
- **Disturbance Rejection**: In disturbance tests involving stick pokes, backward tossing, or water surface agitation (8 trials in total), the fish recovered and reached the target in 7 trials.
A few failure cases occurred at 90° to 120° laterally, but these were caused by physical turn-radius limits imposed by the TG's turning bias cap, rather than a failure of closed-loop tracking.

### VI-D Why Did Transfer Succeed? Spectral Analysis
A power spectral density analysis of tail velocity revealed that in real hardware identification swimming, 92% of the power was concentrated below 4 Hz. The TG policy maintained 97% of its spectral power below 4 Hz, safely remaining inside the model's valid envelope. In contrast, unconstrained Direct Action dropped to only 44% of power below 4 Hz, squandering over half its energy in unmodeled high frequencies. Adding a simple first-order low-pass filter to Direct Action kept forward swimming within bounds, but dropped to 68% in-band power during 14 episodes involving backing up or sharp turns. This confirms that structural frequency capping via the TG is essential.

captions.F7: Hardware swimming trajectories in the outdoor pool. (A) Static target reaching trials showing initial distance, closest approach, and elapsed time. The robot effortlessly reaches targets under stick disturbances, backward releases, and out-of-distribution rearward goals. (B) Trajectory of dynamic tracking (solid line) following a manually moved target along a figure-8 path (dashed line).

sections.heading: Discussion: Should physics live in the simulator, or inside the controller?
sections.summary: RL policies will relentlessly exploit physical flaws in a simulator. Understanding the validity envelope of low-fidelity models and constraining the controller's action space enables robust hardware transfer without demanding excessive simulation accuracy.
sections.details:
The insights of this work extend beyond robotic fish to robotics as a whole: an RL policy will always exploit any physical phenomenon the simulator cannot distinguish. Because stateless fluid models cannot distinguish between amplitude and frequency trade-offs, an unconstrained policy inevitably retreats into high-frequency flutter. Low-cost simulators are valid only within the specific regime where they were identified (here, moderate-amplitude, moderate-frequency undulations); stepping outside returns false physics.

The crucial realization is that instead of engineering complex vortex calculations into the simulator to seal the loophole, the authors bounded the controller frequency so it simply cannot access that loophole. Intriguingly, an unintended parameter discrepancy during hardware deployment caused a 2.7x mismatch in TG amplitude scaling and a 1.5x shift in frequency bounds, alongside an actuator model far stiffer than reality; yet the physical fish swam without issue. Because the policy observes error vectors in the robot's local frame rather than absolute coordinates, and because the action space was constrained to safe swimming gaits, feedback control easily absorbed the parameter discrepancies.

A similar lesson emerged during system identification. Early identification runs yielded unphysical parameter sets where mass distribution and fluid drag inverted swimming directions, moving backward under forward gaits. Locking in inertial properties from CAD beforehand prevented this artifact. This follows the exact same philosophy as the controller constraint: never grant unneeded degrees of freedom to parameters that should not have them.

sections.heading: Conclusion & Outlook: How simple simulators unlock the future of soft robotics
sections.summary: This work proves that even the simplest stateless fluid simulator can achieve advanced zero-shot transfer for a soft underactuated fish when paired with band-limited action spaces and careful identification. Future directions include flexible constraint designs and systematic reachability maps.
sections.details:
This study demonstrated that a single RL policy trained purely in the cheapest, fastest stateless fluid simulator can achieve general closed-loop zero-shot control on a real soft, underactuated robotic fish. Grounding the simulator through two independent identifications (tail stiffness in air, fluid parameters in water) and guiding the policy within the valid envelope via a band-limited Trajectory Generator (TG) were the cornerstones of this success.

The authors outline three key directions for future work:
- **More Flexible Constraints**: Moving beyond rigid harmonic cuts toward directly identifying the boundary of the simulator's validity envelope, applying flexible constraints that unlock the robot's full agile capabilities.
- **Quantitative Reachability Maps**: Transitioning beyond manually placed targets to construct comprehensive, unbiased reachability maps across uniform target grids.
- **Targeted Disturbance Training**: Systematically injecting random external forces into training to deliberately cultivate and amplify the disturbance rejection observed here.

Rather than asking "how much physics must we pack into the simulator?", asking "how much physics can we offload to constraints inside the controller?" represents a mindset shift that could unlock intelligent control for a vast array of soft robots without waiting for heavy fluid and contact solvers.

takeaways: Even low-fidelity simulators can achieve successful zero-shot hardware transfer if the policy's action space is constrained (band-limited) to the simulator's valid operational envelope.
Because RL ruthlessly exploits simulation loopholes (such as high-frequency flutter in stateless fluid models), designing structured priors into the action space serves as an indispensable defense.

System identification should be staged rather than executed all at once; isolating structural stiffness (in air) from hydrodynamics (in water) prevents unphysical parameter distortion and sign reversals.
Framing controller observations around relative error vectors and restricting actions to safe gait parameters yields immense robustness against actuator modeling errors and scale mismatches.
limitations: The Trajectory Generator (TG) constraints were somewhat rigid; saturation in turning bias introduced physical turning-radius limits that prevented sharp turns toward lateral or rear targets (90° to 120°).
Unconstrained Direct Action policies were not deployed in the physical pool, leaving direct hardware verification of whether unconstrained policies unconditionally fail as an open question.
Target reaching performance in the pool was reported as aggregate metrics over manually placed targets, rather than an unbiased, comprehensive evaluation across a uniformly sampled spatial grid.
